name: Defence & Trade
whatThisGrades: Federal action on defence spending and trade diversification away from U.S. reliance.
status: NATO 2.01% met. Trade diversification measurable: US share fell from 75.9% to 71.7%.
judgmentCall: High grade rests on defence delivery; trade gains are discounted because some improvement is market-driven.
judgmentDetail: The A- is not a blanket endorsement of the whole file. Defence spending clears the published NATO 2% threshold, while trade diversification improves enough to help the grade. Judgment enters in discounting the trade-side gain because the U.S. trade shock helped produce some diversification, and in stopping short of A because the 3.5% defence pathway is not funded.
construct: The degree to which the federal government has met its stated defence spending commitments and diversified Canada's trade relationships away from single-market dependency.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Defence target sustained and trade diversification materially improved away from single-market dependency.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: A- rather than A reflects Canada meeting but not materially exceeding the 2% defence floor, while trade diversification remains partly market-driven and the 3.5% target lacks a funded pathway.

activeModifiers.name: External Constraint
activeModifiers.reason: The trade war simultaneously creates the diversification problem and drives some of the measured improvement, so trade gains should not be treated as purely policy-caused.

thresholds.criteria: NATO spending is confirmed at or above 2.0% of GDP and the non-U.S. export share improves by roughly five points or more, with the diversification holding beyond one-month volatility.
NATO 2% is reached or a funded pathway is in place, and the non-U.S. export share improves by roughly one to five points with corridor, procurement, or agreement execution underway.
Defence spending is rising but still below target, or trade diversification is measurable but modest and not yet durable.
Defence spending is flat or below target and trade dependence on the U.S. is unchanged or worsening.
Defence spending is cut and trade dependence deepens.

scoring.scopeNote: Intentionally keeps defence delivery and trade diversification in one file because both sit in the government's national-security and economic-resilience envelope. Read the defence and trade sub-scores with the headline because the two halves move at different speeds.
guardrails: Confirm defence spending from NATO or equivalent official tables, not from domestic political claims alone.
Use annual trade-share movement rather than single-month export volatility when judging diversification.
The defence sub-score anchors the file; trade modifies the headline and should not hide a widening divergence between the two.
If one sub-score rises while the other falls, or the gap between them widens by one full notch, for two consecutive monthly review cycles, promote the split shadow into live separate files.

up.text: 3.5% defence target gets a funded pathway
US export share drops below 68%

rationale: The government set a specific NATO target, funded it ($81.8B over 5 years), and delivered on timeline — NATO confirmed all allies met the 2% target for the first time in 2025 (Canada at 2.01% per NATO expenditure tables). Trade diversification produced measurable results: US export share fell 4.2 percentage points to 71.7% in 2025, the lowest since the early 1980s; non-US goods exports rose 17.2% to an all-time high (Global Affairs Canada). The A- rather than A reflects Canada meeting but not materially exceeding the 2% floor. Policy Options flags the 3.5% GDP defence target is unfunded long-term.

promises.evidence: Announced in Budget 2025. Fund structure being designed. No disbursements yet.
Policy framework announced. Implementation underway across departments.
Announced but not yet launched. No timeline confirmed.

perspectives.critics: Policy Options: the 3.5% GDP defence target cannot be financed without tax increases or structural deficits. NDP and labour groups: $81.8B for defence while housing, healthcare, and childcare remain underfunded is a priorities failure, not a win.
perspectives.defenders: Fraser Institute and NATO allies confirm this is the most significant Canadian defence achievement since the Cold War. Trade diversification is measurable: US export share fell from 75.9% (2024) to 71.7% (2025), and non-US goods exports rose 17.2% to an all-time high (Global Affairs Canada).

defence.rationale: NATO 2% met and confirmed by NATO Secretary General Annual Report. $81.8B committed. Procurement advancing.

trade.label: Trade Diversification
trade.rationale: US export share fell 4.2 percentage points to 71.7% in 2025, the lowest since the early 1980s (Global Affairs Canada, December 2025 report). name: Major Projects
whatThisGrades: How well the federal machinery for approving and delivering major infrastructure is working.
status: 16-project MPO cohort across 3 tranches. 4 projects currently sit above designated status, but only 2 have documented post-designation movement. National interest designation unused.
judgmentCall: Grade rests on documented post-designation movement, not announcement count or project desirability.
judgmentDetail: This grade does not score whether each project is good policy. It scores the federal delivery machinery: the defined MPO cohort, later-dated movement after designation, and use of the national-interest power. Judgment enters in excluding same-day promoted-stage labels from the advancement count and in applying a credit-claiming penalty where the government overstates ownership of pre-existing project progress.
construct: The effectiveness of federal institutional machinery for infrastructure project delivery.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Pipeline exists with 16 projects in the MPO cohort, but fewer than 30% show documented post-designation advancement, and the signature national-interest power remains unused.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: Current C includes a credit-claiming penalty. Without that documented penalty for overstating ownership of pre-existing projects, the raw assessment would sit at C+.

activeModifiers.name: Credit-claiming penalty
activeModifiers.reason: Most projects in the cohort are pre-existing private-sector initiatives (LNG Canada Phase 2, Crawford Nickel, etc.) being expedited rather than new federal projects, and documented overclaiming pulls the raw assessment down from C+ to C.

activeModifiers.name: Timing Fairness
activeModifiers.reason: Infrastructure is multi-year and the MPO is still young, but the machinery itself is already gradeable on cohort progress.

thresholds.criteria: ≥50% of the MPO cohort shows documented advancement of ≥2 stages from designated, OR at least one project completes a full MPO cycle with documented timeline acceleration versus the pre-MPO baseline.
≥30% of the MPO cohort shows documented post-designation advancement, with at least one project in approved / permitted / under construction status.
Pipeline exists with a defined cohort, but <30% of projects show documented post-designation advancement, and no project has completed a full MPO cycle. National-interest designation unused.
Pipeline exists but no documented post-designation stage advancement is visible, OR projects are being withdrawn from the MPO process, OR the framework is being bypassed.
No functioning institutional reform is in place and the federal approval environment worsens versus the inherited baseline.

scoring.scopeNote: Grades federal approval machinery and cohort progress, not whether any specific project is normatively good or bad. Stage advancement is measured against the published stageGates ladder (designated → reviewed → approved → permitted → under_construction → completed), but only later-dated movement after referral counts toward the cohort-advancement thresholds.
guardrails: Pre-existing pipeline value does not count as new federal delivery on its own.
A referred project is not the same as a completed MPO cycle or a verified timeline gain.
Use of the national-interest designation or a documented approval-time improvement is the clearest sign that the machinery is changing outcomes.
Once enough projects reach the permitted / under-construction stages, track median approval time against the MPO's two-year target as the primary acceleration metric.
Projects that appear in the cohort with a promoted stage on the same day they are referred do not count as post-designation advancement until a later recorded transition is visible.
scoring.modifierExpiry: Timing Fairness partly applies while the MPO is still inside its first full project cycle. Until then, institution-building and cohort progress count more than completions, but announcements still do not count as delivery.

up.text: ≥30% of the cohort shows documented post-designation advancement (currently 2 of 16 ≈ 13%)
First project completes a full MPO cycle
First use of national interest designation

down.text: Cohort progress reverses (project moved back to designated from a higher stage)
Evidence the framework is being bypassed

rationale: The Major Projects Office is a real institutional innovation with potentially transformative powers (Building Canada Act, C-5). The cohort has expanded across three tranches to 16 projects, and 4 of 16 projects currently sit above designated status as of April 2026. But only 2 of 16 (~13%) show documented post-designation advancement in the recorded cohort data: Contrecœur Terminal broke ground April 9, 2026, and Darlington New Nuclear carries a later-dated approval / financing milestone. North Coast Transmission Line and Mackenzie Valley Highway have promoted stage labels in tranche-announcement sources, but not a later recorded transition after cohort entry, so they are not yet counted toward the B threshold. The remaining 12 projects sit in initial designated status. The national interest designation has never been used. The $126B headline figure primarily represents pre-existing private-sector investment decisions. The Fraser Institute and Angus Reid both found the government overstated its role. Documented cohort progress therefore sits well below the 30% threshold for B, so the C grade holds. Note: the credit-claiming penalty modifier (-0.3 GPA) is reflected in the current C grade. Without the penalty, the raw assessment would be C+, reduced to C based on documented overclaiming of pre-existing projects by Fraser Institute and Angus Reid.

name: Fiscal Health
whatThisGrades: Federal fiscal trajectory — is the spending and deficit path sustainable and credible?
status: Deficit $66.9B projected in the Spring Economic Update. PBO says new measures offset most post-2025-26 fiscal room. PBO gives 7.5% chance of meeting the original Budget 2025 targets.
judgmentCall: Low grade rests on fiscal-path credibility, not whether individual programs are worthwhile.
judgmentDetail: The D grade is driven by the deficit path, the absence of a credible medium-term anchor, and independent confidence in the stated targets. Judgment enters in weighing strategically justified defence spending against the overall sustainability problem: worthwhile spending can still worsen the fiscal grade if the plan does not show how it will be paid for.
construct: The sustainability of the federal fiscal trajectory and the credibility of the medium-term fiscal plan.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Deficit remains above a sustainable range, the medium-term anchor is not credible, and independent confidence in the fiscal path is low.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: Current D reflects a large projected deficit, only 7.5% PBO confidence in the stated path, and rating pressure warnings despite strategically justified defence spending.

activeModifiers.name: External Constraint
activeModifiers.reason: Trade-war-era defence spending is strategically justified, but it does not excuse broader discretionary fiscal expansion such as the gas tax suspension.

thresholds.criteria: Budget is balanced or in surplus, debt-to-GDP is declining, PBO confidence is above 80%, and no rating-pressure warning is active.
Deficit is below 2% of GDP, a medium-term anchor is published, PBO confidence is between 50% and 80%, and no active rating warning is live.
Deficit is 2% to 4% of GDP, an anchor is published but PBO confidence is only 25% to 50%, or at least one rating agency is flagging a material caveat.
Deficit is above 4% of GDP, PBO confidence is below 25%, the anchor is absent or repeatedly missed, and rating pressure is active.
An actual downgrade or clear fiscal-crisis dynamic emerges.

scoring.scopeNote: Grades sustainability and credibility of the fiscal path, not whether any one spending item is morally worthwhile.
guardrails: Separate debt level from debt trajectory; manageable current debt does not rescue an unsustainable path.
A strategic defence-spending case can explain part of the expansion but not the rest of the fiscal package.
Use PBO confidence and rating-agency language as the credibility check, not ministerial framing.

up.text: PBO confidence rises above 25%
Fitch removes its warning

down.sourceLabel: Fitch / Moody's / S&P event-driven rating source

rationale: The Spring Economic Update lowers the projected FY 2025-26 deficit to $66.9B from Budget 2025's $78.3B, helped by stronger income-tax revenues and lower direct program expenses. But PBO's assessment says new policy measures offset almost all fiscal room after 2025-26, leaving the 2029-30 deficit effectively unchanged from Budget 2025. Fitch maintained its AA+ rating with a stable outlook after Budget 2025 but warned that persistent fiscal expansion could increase rating pressure over the medium term. The PBO gives only 7.5% probability the original deficit-to-GDP path will decline as projected. Defence spending is strategically justified, but the broader fiscal package still lacks a credible anchor.

perspectives.critics: C.D. Howe: every GST dollar now goes to debt servicing. PBO gives 7.5% probability of meeting deficit targets — in any other context that plan gets rejected. Fitch maintained AA+ but warned persistent deficits could increase rating pressure. La Presse: the gas tax suspension costs $2.4B the government cannot afford.
perspectives.defenders: IMF and IFSD note Canada's debt-to-GDP ratio remains manageable by international standards. Defence spending is strategically necessary during a trade war. The operating/capital budget split is a legitimate framework innovation. Kevin Page: "There is no fiscal crisis."

nextTrigger: April 28, 2026 economic update from Finance Minister Champagne. PBO spring fiscal outlook. Fitch/Moody's review.

name: Economic Policy Response
whatThisGrades: Federal action on Canada's productivity and competitiveness — investment, innovation, jobs, wages.
status: Structural productivity weakness is inherited. The file now tracks tax, trade, regulatory, and funding levers explicitly, but fewer than two core levers are at authorized-or-executing stage and business investment remains near-flat.
judgmentCall: Low grade reflects execution status across policy levers, with inherited productivity weakness treated as context.
judgmentDetail: The grade is about the federal response, not Canada's inherited productivity level. Judgment enters in deciding which levers count as execution-ready: announced funds and frameworks are not treated the same as Treasury Board-authorized programs, live tax or regulatory changes, or measurable internal-trade and permitting movement.
construct: The federal posture on productivity and competitiveness across funding, tax, regulatory, and trade levers.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Instruments are still mostly announced rather than Treasury Board-authorized or in live execution, and business investment remains near-flat without a durable turn.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: Current D reflects a real policy response that has not yet cleared the execution bar: key funds are still more announced than live, business investment remains near-flat, and major domestic barriers remain unresolved.

activeModifiers.name: Timing Fairness
activeModifiers.reason: This is a long-lag file, so the grade assesses trajectory and adequacy of response rather than inherited GDP per capita outcomes.

activeModifiers.name: External Constraint
activeModifiers.reason: The trade war constrains business investment decisions, but it does not resolve the domestic productivity barriers that still sit inside federal control.

thresholds.criteria: At least two core productivity levers are enacted or Treasury Board-authorized, at least one is in live execution or disbursement, business investment rises for two or more consecutive quarters, and independent assessment judges the trajectory improved.
At least two core levers are funded or authorized, at least one is in live execution, and business investment is no longer declining over two consecutive quarters.

At least one core lever is funded or authorized and others are designed or announced, but business investment remains flat or only marginally positive and measurable productivity gains are not yet visible.

Instruments are still mostly announced rather than authorized or executing, fewer than two core levers are clearly funded or authorized, and business investment is still near-flat without a durable two-quarter turn.
No material federal productivity response through funding, tax, regulatory, or trade action.

scoring.scopeNote: Grades the federal response, not the inherited outcome level. The card now tracks tax, trade, regulatory, and permitting-adjacent breadth checks alongside funding instruments.
guardrails: Announcements alone do not count. Require Treasury Board authorization, legislation, or confirmed disbursement before a new instrument can lift the grade.
Business investment is the main live outcome check. Two consecutive quarters are required before treating a turn as real.
For this file, core levers currently mean AI compute, critical minerals execution, interprovincial trade implementation, regulatory-review execution, and productivity-tax competitiveness measures.
Permitting, tax, electricity, and regulatory barriers remain part of the response question even when external conditions are poor.
scoring.modifierExpiry: Timing Fairness is active on this long-lag file and expires March 14, 2027. After that date, outcome metrics weigh more directly in the band pick.

up.text: AI compute fund begins actual disbursement confirmed by Treasury Board or PBO
Business investment turns positive for two or more consecutive quarters
up.sourceLabel: StatsCan GDP, income and expenditure — Q4 2025

down.text: Additional major fund announced without Treasury Board authorization

down.sourceLabel: StatsCan GDP, income and expenditure — Q4 2025

rationale: This dimension grades the government's productivity and competitiveness posture rather than the inherited GDP-per-capita level, which reflects a decade of underinvestment. The file now tracks non-spending levers explicitly: Budget 2025's productivity super-deduction lowers the marginal effective tax rate on new business investment, Bill C-5 is the live internal-trade instrument, and Treasury Board's Red Tape Review has identified hundreds of regulatory initiatives. But fewer than two core levers have clearly cleared the authorization-or-execution bar, no permitting-acceleration tool has yet been used, and business investment rose only 0.3% in 2025 after repeated weak quarters. The grade reflects whether the policy mix is becoming broad and executable enough to change the trajectory, recognizing that outcomes will take time to move.

Canada produces 10 of 12 NATO defence-critical minerals.

promises.evidence: Announced but reports not yet public.

perspectives.critics: If Carney is the credibility candidate — the one markets trust — why has business investment not turned after 13 months? Permitting, tax rates, electricity costs, and regulatory uncertainty remain unresolved. OECD long-term projections rank Canada last or near-last among 38 members for per-capita GDP growth through 2060 (Fraser Institute / BCBC analysis of OECD data).
perspectives.defenders: Budget 2025 adds a productivity super-deduction, internal-trade legislation is enacted, and the Red Tape Review is now producing a government-wide regulatory pipeline. Productivity is a decade-long structural problem, so a 13-month score should focus on whether the response mix is broadening rather than expecting immediate GDP-per-capita reversal.

nextTrigger: Treasury Board authorization or first confirmed disbursement for AI compute. Q1 2026 business investment data. Any authorization or disbursement evidence for critical minerals instruments.
inherited: GDP per capita declined 2.0% from 2020-2024. Business investment falling since 2006. R&D at half the US rate. Population-driven growth masked per-capita decline for a decade.

name: Affordability Response
whatThisGrades: Federal response to household cost pressure — groceries, tariff-driven costs, targeted relief.
status: Government affordability measures cover <20% of household cost increases. Grocery Code voluntary. Tariff costs add $1,450-$2,000/yr per household. Grade reflects federal policy response, not global price levels.
judgmentCall: Low grade reflects federal relief versus measured household cost pressure, not a verdict on global prices.
judgmentDetail: The D- grade scores the adequacy of federal action against documented cost pressure. Judgment enters in matching relief scale to the identified annual burden, treating voluntary grocery measures as weaker than enforceable ones, and separating federal policy response from global price shocks that Ottawa does not fully control.
construct: Adequacy of the federal policy response to household cost pressure from groceries, tariffs, and targeted relief.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Federal relief covers less than 20% of estimated annual cost increase.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: D- per rubric: near-total failure; relief covers a negligible share of the identified cost and structural drivers remain unaddressed.

activeModifiers.name: External Constraint
activeModifiers.reason: Tariffs add $1,450-$2,000/yr per household. Per rubric condition, the modifier applies only when the government's response is adequate given the constraint. Response judged inadequate, so the modifier was not applied.

thresholds.criteria: Federal relief offsets more than 80% of the identified annual household cost increase and at least one mandatory grocery-competition or market-conduct reform is enacted.
Federal relief offsets 40% to 80% of the cost increase and at least one enforceable competition or compliance measure is in force.
Federal relief offsets 20% to 40% of the cost increase and targeted programs are live, but the competition response remains voluntary or partial.
Federal relief offsets less than 20% of the cost increase, voluntary or narrow measures dominate, and food insecurity remains elevated or rising.
No material federal relief or competition response is in place.

judgmentDetail: The D grade is driven by the policy framework: major reversals, no funded replacement strategy, shrinking institutional capacity, and an acknowledged gap to 2030 targets. construct: The scale and coherence of the federal environmental policy framework.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: Major environmental reversals occurred without a credible replacement strategy, targets are acknowledged as out of reach, and institutional capacity is shrinking.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: Current D reflects large policy reversals without a funded replacement framework, declining ECCC capacity, and an openly deteriorating path to the 2030 target.

activeModifiers.name: External Constraint

thresholds.criteria: The major climate framework is maintained or strengthened, no major reversal is left unreplaced, and independent assessment says the pathway is at least roughly three-quarters of the way to the 2030 target.

Major reversals occur, but a funded replacement strategy exists and at least one major instrument or functional substitute remains intact.

Major reversals occur without a funded replacement strategy, Canada is tracking below half of the required 2030 reduction or the government concedes the targets are out of reach, and ECCC capacity is shrinking.
The major climate framework is effectively dismantled or policy choices actively accelerate emissions.

scoring.scopeNote: Grades the climate-policy framework and replacement strategy, not the carbon-pricing instrument itself and not short-run emissions noise.
guardrails: Use replacement strategy, budget capacity, and preserved instruments rather than rhetoric when judging the file.

name: Immigration
whatThisGrades: Federal immigration policy — permanent resident levels, temporary residents, and student/worker streams.
status: Sharp immigration contraction. Correction is substantial and necessary. Long-term model not yet defined (tracked as next grade trigger).
judgmentCall: Plus grade credits a real levels correction but holds back because the long-term model is unresolved.
judgmentDetail: The C+ grade gives credit for a substantial correction to an overloaded system while stopping short of B because the durable model is not defined. Judgment enters in treating the correction as necessary rather than punitive, and in weighing unresolved sector, service, and long-term planning risks against the clear execution of lower levels.
construct: The adequacy and coherence of the federal immigration level correction.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: The correction has been executed sharply and at real scale, but the long-term model is not yet defined and downside risks remain only partly addressed.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: Current C+ reflects a substantial correction that addresses a real overload problem while still leaving the long-term design unresolved and exposing service-sensitive sectors to downside risk.

thresholds.criteria: A published long-term model aligns levels with absorption capacity, temporary residents are on or below the 5% path, and major service impacts are contained.

No material correction occurs, or the pullback causes documented service failure without mitigation.
Intake management collapses: no coherent model is in place and serious service disruption or uncontrolled growth is evident.

scoring.scopeNote: Grades alignment and management of immigration levels, not whether high or low immigration is ideologically preferable.
guardrails: Operational permit, admission, and population data matter more than speeches or intentions.

The right-sized long-term model has not been defined, which is tracked as the primary trigger for the next grade movement rather than a current grading input. rationale: This dimension measures the government's cross-cutting capacity to convert announcements into measurable results across its five highest-profile files: defence (NATO 2%), housing (Build Canada Homes), major projects (MPO), climate (policy framework), and immigration (levels reduction). It is deliberately narrow — it grades execution machinery, not policy merit. Defence shows the government can deliver when focused. Housing and climate show it cannot yet deliver at scale on domestic files. The 40,000 public service job cuts while pursuing an ambitious agenda raise structural capacity questions, a concern reinforced by C.D. Howe's analysis of a worsening executive-to-rank-and-file ratio.

rationale: The Carney government made specific commitments on defence (NATO 2%), trade diversification, carbon tax elimination, immigration reduction, and interprovincial reform — and delivered on all of them. These are genuine achievements. However, housing targets have been scaled back, climate commitments were largely reversed rather than delivered, and the pattern across domestic files is consistent: ambitious announcements followed by results that fall short. The tracker read reflects real delivery on priority files alongside persistent underdelivery on household-impact files. Note: Promise Delivery is a derivative tracker. Movements that are already captured in home dimensions (e.g., housing delivery moving Housing Supply) should not independently move this tracker. This dimension tracks the cumulative pattern of commitment fulfillment as a political accountability measure, not as an independent policy performance indicator.
